title: Talk to Your Students
author: Michael G. Wagner
summary: Wagner borrows a cardiologist's advice to doctors, "Talk to your patients," and applies it to teachers in the age of AI. He follows Dr. Rohin Francis's video through several arguments: a good history tells you more than a scan, testing everyone just in case produces wrong results, one ambiguous flag leads to more scrutiny, and professionals must sometimes say no instead of deferring. Each maps onto schools, where running every essay through an AI detector is the full-body scan and recording software is the next link in the chain. He argues that identical student work can mean very different things, and that only a conversation reveals what the student brought to it. He admits the analogy has limits, since students are not patients and in teaching the conversation is part of the learning itself. He ends on the surgeon's rule that the best practitioner knows when not to act, and that the teaching version is to start with a conversation instead of an investigation.
points: Ask students how they used AI before anything is graded and with no threat attached, because those conversations reveal more about student thinking than any detector.
AI detectors face a built-in trade-off between catching more AI text and wrongly flagging honest students, so universal scanning is the school version of over-testing.
A single detector flag cascades into integrity meetings and recording software, so conversations must not become another link in that chain.
Teachers should be willing to say no and make students defend claims, because sycophantic models will not push back.
Responsibility for what happens to the student stays with the teacher, however many tasks are handed to a model.
quotes: Teaching works much the same way. An identical piece of work can mean very different things depending on who produced it. Take a student who asks a chatbot for a summary.

Those conversations only work when the possibility of an academic integrity case is off the table. But once that threat is gone, those conversations tell me more about how students think than any AI detector ever has.

Human and machine writing overlap, so every school has to choose between catching more AI text and wrongly flagging more honest students. Better engineering can shift that trade-off around, but it can’t make it go away.

In a school, the scarce resource is the teacher’s attention. Every hour spent investigating a flag on an honest student’s essay is an hour that doesn’t go to the student who has been lost since September.

Language models are prone to what researchers call sycophancy, which means they tend to go along with whatever the user already seems to believe. Over a long chat, that can slowly turn a student’s half-formed guess into something that reads like settled fact
In medicine, talking with a patient is mostly a way to reach a diagnosis. In teaching, the conversation is often part of the learning itself.
A teacher can hand many tasks to a model, yet the responsibility for what happens to the student stays with the teacher.
A good teacher knows how to investigate a suspicious essay. The best teacher knows when not to, and knows to start with a conversation instead.
context: The same output can reflect understanding or avoidance, and only asking tells them apart.
Trust is the precondition for honest accounts of how AI was used.
Detection accuracy is a policy trade-off, not an engineering problem to be solved away.
Investigating false flags consumes attention that struggling students need.
Agreeable models can harden a half-formed guess into apparent fact.
Student conversations serve learning, not only diagnosis in the author's argument.
Delegating tasks to AI does not delegate accountability in the author's argument.
The closing line sets conversation ahead of investigation in the author's argument.
